generalizedRange: Steppes and semi-deserts of Central Asia — Kazakhstan above all, with small herds in Russia, Uzbekistan and Mongolia
hook: In 2003: 21,000. In 2015, 200,000 died in three weeks. Today: millions.

story.text: The saiga’s nose is an inflated, drooping tube: it warms air at minus 40 on the winter steppe and filters dust at plus 40 in summer.
It grazed beside mammoths; the megafauna went, the saiga stayed, still migrating more than a thousand kilometers a year.
Only males carry the ridged amber horns, and those horns are why they were hunted: within a decade numbers fell more than 95 percent, to about 21,000 by 2003.
In May 2015 a common bacterium, Pasteurella multocida, killed more than 200,000 saiga in three weeks — some 62 percent of the world’s — after unusually warm, humid days in Betpak-Dala.
Then the steppe refilled: rangers, spring aerial counts and five million protected hectares later, Kazakhstan’s 2024 census found 2,833,600.
On 11 December 2023 the IUCN moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened.
Abundance has its own arithmetic: in 2025 Kazakhstan culled about 196,000 saiga to protect farmland, and CITES let it export 10,000 kilograms of horn a year for three years.
Scientists warn the die-offs recur, and conservationists fear reopened trade will pull demand toward the small herds of Mongolia, Russia and Uzbekistan.
To witness the saiga antelope is to see a species come back within a single human lifetime — and to keep counting.

stats.size: Sheep-sized · 2–2.6 ft at the shoulder · 66–99 lbs (30–45 kg)
stats.diet: Grazer — grasses, herbs, lichens & low shrubs, 100+ plant species
stats.populationEstimate: 2,833,600 in Kazakhstan (about 99 percent of the species)
stats.populationAsOf: 2024 · per ACBK aerial census / Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative

reproduction.text: Females breed in their first year; after 139 to 152 days about two-thirds bear twins, in late April and May — so a herd can grow 35 to 40 percent in a good year.

insight.text: The bacterium that killed 200,000 saiga in 2015 is an ordinary opportunist that had struck the same ground in 1981 and 1988; what changed was the weather — a run of unusually warm, humid days.

programs.title: Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative
programs.summary: Since 2006 has counted Kazakhstan’s saiga from the air each spring, GPS-collared herds, run ranger and aerial anti-poaching patrols, and helped the government protect some 5 million hectares of steppe — the 2024 Earthshot Prize winner for Protect & Restore Nature.

programs.title: Saiga population monitoring
programs.summary: Coordinates line-transect counts, satellite tagging and drone trials across the five range states, working with ACBK in Kazakhstan and WWF-Mongolia’s community conservationists to track the smaller herds.
